title: Three weeks off, one technicality: how a chef's hand injury nearly killed his TPD claim
full_text:
What happened: AIA Australia denied a chef's TPD claim because a separate hand injury interrupted his work hours in the three months before his disabling back condition
Who's involved: AIA Australia (insurer), Club Super (superannuation fund), Port Curtis Sailing Club (employer)
What's at stake: a total and permanent disability benefit under a group life policy, amount not specified in the judgment
Why it matters: the ruling limits insurers' ability to use work-status eligibility thresholds to deny TPD claims when the shortfall had no connection to the disabling condition
Where it stands: appeal dismissed on October 30, 2026; costs to be heard separately
He worked 38 hours a week as a club chef - except for the three weeks an unrelated hand injury kept him home. That gap was enough for AIA Australia to deny his total and permanent disability claim.
The Queensland Court of Appeal disagreed. In a unanimous decision delivered on October 30, 2026, the court dismissed AIA Australia's appeal and upheld a lower court finding that the insurer could not rely on the work-hours shortfall to refuse cover. The reason: a provision in federal insurance law - s 54 of the Insurance Contracts Act 1984 - stops insurers from denying claims based on technicalities that had nothing to do with the actual loss.
The timeline tells the story. The worker joined the Port Curtis Sailing Club as a chef in December 2014 and became a permanent full-time employee in February 2015, working 38 hours or more each week. He joined the Club Super superannuation fund on February 11, 2015. Within weeks, a hand tendon injury requiring two surgeries forced him off work from late March until early July 2015. He returned to full duties. Then, on September 14, 2015 - a little over two months later - severe back pain, muscle spasms and other injuries ended his working life for good.
His employer terminated him. Six months on, medical evidence confirmed he was unlikely to ever work again in any role suited to his education, training and experience.
The superannuation fund lodged a TPD claim with AIA Australia on his behalf. AIA Australia, which had taken over as the group life insurer on April 1, 2015 while the worker was still recovering from the hand injury, said no.
The policy required an insured member to have been "continuously working for 15 hours or more per week" in the three months before becoming disabled. The hand injury meant the worker fell short of that threshold - even though he worked 38 hours a week for 10 of the 13 weeks in that window and averaged 31 hours a week across the full period.
AIA Australia argued the work requirement was fundamental to the type of cover on offer - a way of sorting members into different risk categories, not the kind of clause the law was designed to override.
The court looked past how the clause was drafted and focused on what the policy actually insured: the risk of death, terminal illness or total and permanent disability happening to a covered member. The 15-hour work threshold, the court found, had nothing to do with that core purpose. It was just a timing condition bolted onto the cover - what the judges called "merely a temporal limitation or qualification" on the policy's essential purpose.
That distinction matters. Under a line of High Court authority going back decades, insurers cannot dodge a claim by pointing to a policy condition that has no causal connection to the loss, regardless of how that condition is labelled or where it sits in the policy wording. It does not matter whether the clause is framed as a definition, a condition or an exclusion.
The court also noted that the worker's hand injury - the sole reason for the work-hours gap - had nothing to do with the back condition that destroyed his career. The respondent's evidence, which the court noted approvingly, showed that premiums under the policy were set by age, with no distinction made for how many hours a member worked. No actuarial evidence was offered to suggest that working fewer than 15 hours a week increases the risk of the kind of injury suffered here.
The appeal is dismissed. Costs submissions will be heard separately.
For group insurers and superannuation trustees, the decision is a reminder that work-status eligibility thresholds in TPD definitions may not hold up when the shortfall has no connection to the disabling condition and no bearing on how the premium was priced.
